query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy is derived from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi and is intended to retain a favorable strength–ductility balance in its solidified solid-solution state, but its dynamic behavior across different temperatures and strain rates lacks a theoretical explanation. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could account for this behavior, and what controlled comparison within that regime would distinguish it? Specify predictions relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and a falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the Co‐free FeNiCrMn high‐entropy alloy, removing Co increases the stacking fault energy and alters the balance between dislocation‐mediated slip and deformation twinning. As a result, the alloy’s dynamic mechanical response (strength–ductility balance) across temperatures and strain rates is governed predominantly by temperature‐ and rate‐dependent dislocation mobility rather than twinning. This leads to a strengthening response at low temperatures/high strain rates due to hindered dislocation motion with reduced twinning, while at elevated temperatures/low strain rates enhanced thermal activation promotes more homogeneous slip and ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast, single-phase solid-solution Co‐free FeNiCrMn alloy with a fine, homogeneous microstructure.
generation.intervention: Subject the Co‐free alloy to a series of tensile or compression tests spanning a range of temperatures (e.g., room temperature to ~900 K) and strain rates (from quasi-static ~10^−3 s^−1 up to high strain rates ~10^3 s^−1) while maintaining a controlled and similar microstructure.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted under identical thermal-mechanical conditions for both the Co‐free alloy and a baseline equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloy, ensuring similar grain sizes and absence of secondary phases.
generation.structural_mediator: Altered stacking fault energy that suppresses the formation of deformation twins and modifies the dislocation core and mobility; the resulting microstructural features (twin density and dislocation arrangements) mediate the mechanical response.
generation.mechanism: Removing Co increases the average stacking fault energy, thereby reducing the propensity for deformation twinning. At low temperatures/high strain rates, the higher effective energy barrier limits dislocation glide, leading to a higher yield strength but less capacity for twin-mediated accommodation of plasticity. Conversely, at elevated temperatures/low strain rates, thermal activation overcomes the barrier and facilitates more uniform dislocation slip, restoring ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi baseline, the Co‐free alloy will exhibit a steeper increase in yield strength with decreasing temperature and increasing strain rate (due to more pronounced dislocation pinning) along with a concomitant reduction in twinning activity. This should be observable as distinct differences in the stress–strain curves (e.g., differences in strain hardening rates) and lower twin fractions in microstructural analysis at equivalent testing conditions.
generation.baseline: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy tested under the same thermal and strain-rate conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies within the single-phase solid-solution regime where neither secondary precipitation nor significant grain growth occurs (e.g., temperatures from ~300 K to ~900 K and strain rates from ~10^−3 s^−1 to ~10^3 s^−1).
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative differences in yield strength, strain hardening, and exact twin fractions are uncertain due to interplay of lattice distortion effects and possible local chemical ordering; furthermore, the precise magnitude of the stacking fault energy change upon Co removal is not fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples—one of the Co‐free FeNiCrMn alloy and one of the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloy—with identical processing histories and microstructure. Conduct in situ tensile (or compression) tests over a range of temperatures (e.g., 300 K to 900 K) and strain rates (from ~10^−3 s^−1 to ~10^3 s^−1) while simultaneously characterizing the evolving dislocation structures and twin density using high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and/or in situ neutron diffraction.
measurements: Yield strength and strain-hardening rate from stress–strain curves
Fraction and morphology of deformation twins
Stacking fault energy estimates from independent computational or diffraction-based methods
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If under equivalent testing conditions the Co‐free alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in twin activity and shows a similar temperature and strain-rate dependence of yield strength and ductility as the baseline CoCrFeMnNi alloy, then the hypothesis that increased stacking fault energy and consequent suppression of twinning governs the dynamic behavior will be falsified.

Although practically all metals suffer from such phenomena, the high-entropy alloy (HEA) investigated here seems to be not only less prone to hydrogen embrittlement but it even profits from its presence. HEAs are a new class of materials originally defined as solid metallic solutions composed of five or more principal elements in equimolar or near-equimolar ratios for yielding high configurational entropy. This concept introduces a new path for developing advanced materials with some unique mechanical properties. The five-component equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloy, also referred to as Cantor’s alloy, is one of the most appealing HEAs due to the high thermodynamic stability of its single face-centred cubic (f.c.c.) structure and the excellent mechanical properties under various temperatures. Owing to these features we picked this equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi model HEA for studying its changing mechanical tensile behaviour when exposed to hydrogen. We show that this material is not only resistant to hydrogen embrittlement but we even observe its beneficial role as alloying element as it improves rather than deteriorates both, the material’s strength and ductility. AbstractCrCoNi alloy exhibits a remarkable combination of strength and plastic deformation, even superior to the CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy. We connect the magnetic and mechanical properties of CrCoNi, via a magnetically tunable phase transformation. While both alloys crystallize as single-phase face-centered-cubic (fcc) solid solutions, we find a distinctly lower-energy phase in CrCoNi alloy with a hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structure. Comparing the magnetic configurations of CrCoNi with those of other equiatomic ternary derivatives of CrMnFeCoNi confirms that magnetically frustrated Mn eliminates the fcc-hcp energy difference. This highlights the unique combination of chemistry and magnetic properties in CrCoNi, leading to a fcc-hcp phase transformation that occurs only in this alloy, and is triggered by dislocation slip and interaction with internal boundaries. This phase transformation sets CrCoNi apart from the parent quinary, and its other equiatomic ternary derivatives, and provides a new way for increasing strength without compromising plastic deformation.
